name: Fortran
title: Fortran: numbers, arrays and science
intro: Fortran (FORmula TRANslation) appeared in 1957 and was the first widely used high-level language. It is still a working language in scientific computing: weather and climate models, physics, engineering and many of the fast maths libraries other languages call into are written in it, so it is worth knowing if you work anywhere near numbers. Today's Fortran is a clean, modern language with whole-array operations built in. These lessons use free-form Fortran 2008. Old code from before 1990 (FORTRAN 77) uses fixed columns and capital letters; lesson 1 shows how to recognise it. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.f90 and type gfortran -o hello hello.f90 && ./hello.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.summary: program, print, comments and implicit none.

sections.p: A Fortran program sits between program name and end program name. print '(a)', ... prints a line of text: the part in quotes is a format, and (a) means "a piece of text". ! starts a comment. Always write implicit none at the top; without it, Fortran guesses a type for any name you forget to declare, and a typo silently becomes a new variable.
sections.code:
program hello
  implicit none
  ! Print two lines
  print '(a)', 'Hello, squirrel!'
  print '(a)', 'Nuts are ready.'
end program hello

sections.h: Several items, and the quick form
sections.p: A format can list several items: (a, a) prints two pieces of text with nothing between them. You will also see print *, ..., the quick form that lets the compiler choose the layout. It is handy for debugging, but each compiler spaces it a little differently (gfortran starts each line with a space), so these lessons write the format out.
sections.code:
program join
  implicit none
  print '(a, a)', 'Acorn', 'Bank'
  print '(a, a)', 'Acorn ', 'Bank'
  print *, 'Quick form'
end program join

sections.p: Older code is in fixed form: a C or * in column 1 marks a comment, columns 1 to 5 hold statement labels, a character in column 6 continues the previous line, and statements go in columns 7 to 72. Loops end on a numbered CONTINUE line. Modern compilers still build this code, which is one reason so much of it is still running.

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  print '(a, a)', 'Pay', 'day'
end program q1
practice.why: The format (a, a) prints the two strings right next to each other.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  print '(a)', 'One'
  ! print '(a)', 'Two'
  print '(a)', 'Three'
end program q2
practice.why: The middle line starts with !, so it is a comment and never runs.

options: So every variable must be declared and typos are caught
To make the program run faster
To allow any type in any variable
practice.answer: So every variable must be declared and typos are caught
practice.why: Without it, Fortran gives undeclared names a type from their first letter, so a misspelt name quietly becomes a new variable.

practice.q: Where is Fortran still widely used?
practice.why: Weather, climate, physics and engineering codes, and many fast maths libraries, are written in Fortran.

lessons.title: Variables and formats
lessons.summary: integer, real, character, logical, and the i, f and a edit descriptors.

sections.p: Declarations come first, before any statement. The main types are integer, real, character(len=n) and logical (.true. or .false.). In a format, i0 prints an integer in as few digits as it needs, and a prints text.
sections.code:
program vars
  implicit none
  integer :: nuts
  character(len=8) :: owner
  nuts = 42
  owner = 'Squirrel'
  print '(a, a, i0, a)', owner, ' has ', nuts, ' nuts'
end program vars

sections.p: A plain real has only about 7 significant digits. Scientific code uses 64-bit reals, chosen with a kind: use iso_fortran_env, only: real64, then real(real64), and literals written with _real64. In a format, f8.3 prints a real 8 characters wide with 3 digits after the point, and f0.2 uses just as much width as it needs. With f0, the zero before the point is optional in the standard, and gfortran leaves it out.
sections.code:
program reals
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  real(real64) :: x
  x = 2.0_real64 / 3.0_real64
  print '(f8.3)', x
  print '(f0.2)', x
  print '(f0.10)', x
end program reals

sections.p: parameter makes a named constant that can never change. Text in a character variable is padded with spaces to its full length; trim removes the trailing spaces.
sections.code:
program consts
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: days = 7
  character(len=10) :: tree
  tree = 'Oak'
  print '(a, a, a)', '[', tree, ']'
  print '(a, a, a)', '[', trim(tree), ']'
  print '(i0)', days * 2
end program consts

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  n = 7
  print '(a, i0)', 'n=', n
end program q1
practice.why: i0 prints the integer in as few digits as it needs, with no padding.

practice.code:
program q2
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  real(real64) :: x
  x = 1.0_real64 / 4.0_real64
  print '(f0.3)', x
end program q2
practice.why: f0.3 always prints exactly three digits after the point, so 0.25 becomes .250. With f0, gfortran leaves out the zero before the point.

practice.code:
program q3
  implicit none
  character(len=6) :: w
  w = 'Elm'
  print '(a, a, a)', '<', trim(w), '>'
end program q3
practice.why: w holds Elm followed by three spaces; trim removes them.

practice.q: What does integer, parameter :: n = 10 declare?
options: A named constant that cannot be changed
practice.answer: A named constant that cannot be changed
practice.why: parameter fixes the value at compile time. Assigning to n later is an error.

practice.q: How do you get 64-bit reals in portable modern Fortran?
practice.why: iso_fortran_env gives standard kind names. real*8 is an old extension you will see in legacy code.

lessons.title: Arithmetic
lessons.summary: Integer division, powers, mixed types and intrinsic functions.

sections.p: + - * / work as usual, and ** is a power. Dividing two integers gives an integer and drops the fraction. mod(a, b) is the remainder.
sections.code:
program ints
  implicit none
  print '(i0)', 7 / 2
  print '(i0)', mod(7, 2)
  print '(i0)', 2**10
  print '(i0)', -7 / 2
end program ints

sections.p: If either side is real, the arithmetic is done in real. real(n, real64) converts an integer on purpose, and int(x) cuts a real down to a whole number. The intrinsic functions such as sqrt, abs and exp work on any real kind.
sections.code:
program mixed
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  real(real64) :: x
  n = 7
  x = real(n, real64) / 2
  print '(f0.1)', x
  print '(i0)', int(x)
  print '(f0.6)', sqrt(2.0_real64)
  print '(f0.1)', abs(-3.5_real64)
end program mixed

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  print '(i0)', 9 / 4
end program q1
practice.why: Both sides are integers, so the result is an integer and the .25 is dropped.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  print '(i0)', 3**3
end program q2
practice.why: ** is a power: 3 to the power 3 is 27.

practice.code:
program q3
  implicit none
  print '(i0)', mod(17, 5)
end program q3
practice.why: 17 is 3 fives (15) with 2 left over.

practice.code:
program q4
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  print '(f0.2)', 9 / 4 * 1.0_real64
end program q4
practice.why: Fortran works left to right: 9 / 4 is integer division and gives 2 before the multiplication turns it into a real.

lessons.title: Decisions
lessons.summary: if, else if and select case.

sections.p: if (condition) then ... else if ... else ... end if. Comparisons are == /= < <= > >=, and conditions combine with .and., .or. and .not.. Note that "not equal" is /=.
sections.code:
program check
  implicit none
  integer :: t
  t = 25
  if (t > 30) then
    print '(a)', 'Hot'
  else if (t > 15) then
    print '(a)', 'Mild'
  else
    print '(a)', 'Cold'
  end if
  if (t /= 0 .and. mod(t, 5) == 0) print '(a)', 'Multiple of five'
end program check

sections.p: select case picks one branch by value. A case can list several values or a range written with :, and case default catches the rest.
sections.code:
program grade
  implicit none
  integer :: score
  score = 82
  select case (score)
  case (90:)
    print '(a)', 'A'
  case (80:89)
    print '(a)', 'B'
  case (70:79)
    print '(a)', 'C'
  case default
    print '(a)', 'Try again'
  end select
end program grade

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  n = 10
  if (n > 10) then
    print '(a)', 'big'
  else
    print '(a)', 'small'
  end if
end program q1
practice.why: 10 is not greater than 10, so the else branch runs.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  integer :: d
  d = 6
  select case (d)
  case (1:5)
    print '(a)', 'Weekday'
  case (6, 7)
    print '(a)', 'Weekend'
  case default
    print '(a)', 'No such day'
  end select
end program q2
practice.why: case (6, 7) matches either value. Only one branch runs.

practice.q: How do you write "not equal" in Fortran?
practice.why: Fortran uses /= (or the old .ne.). != starts a comment in Fortran.
A range with no upper end is open on that side.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: Counted do loops, do while, exit and cycle.

sections.p: do i = first, last counts up by 1, and a third number gives the step. The last value is included. The loop ends at end do.
sections.code:
program counting
  implicit none
  integer :: i
  do i = 1, 3
    print '(a, i0)', 'Step ', i
  end do
  do i = 10, 0, -5
    print '(i0)', i
  end do
end program counting

sections.p: do while (condition) checks before each pass. Inside any loop, exit leaves it at once and cycle skips to the next pass. A bare do with an exit inside is a common way to loop until something happens.
sections.code:
program control
  implicit none
  integer :: n, i
  n = 1
  do while (n < 20)
    n = n * 2
  end do
  print '(i0)', n
  do i = 1, 10
    if (mod(i, 2) == 0) cycle
    if (i > 7) exit
    print '(i0)', i
  end do
end program control

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  integer :: i
  do i = 2, 6, 2
    print '(i0)', i
  end do
end program q1
practice.why: The loop counts from 2 in steps of 2, and the last value, 6, is included.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  integer :: i, total
  total = 0
  do i = 1, 4
    total = total + i
  end do
  print '(i0)', total
end program q2

program q3
  implicit none
  integer :: i
  do i = 1, 5
    if (i == 3) cycle
    print '(i0)', i
  end do
end program q3
practice.why: cycle skips the rest of the pass when i is 3, then the loop carries on.

practice.q: What does exit do inside a do loop?
practice.why: exit jumps to just after end do. cycle is the one that skips to the next pass, and stop ends the program.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Declaring arrays, 1-based indexes and whole-array operations.

sections.p: integer :: a(5) declares five integers. Indexes start at 1. [ ... ] builds an array from a list, and the format (*(i0, 1x)) repeats "an integer and one space" for every item.
sections.code:
program arrays
  implicit none
  integer :: nuts(3)
  nuts = [12, 30, 5]
  print '(i0)', nuts(1)
  nuts(3) = nuts(3) + 1
  print '(*(i0, 1x))', nuts
end program arrays

sections.p: Arithmetic works on whole arrays at once, element by element, with no loop. Intrinsics such as sum, maxval and size work on a whole array, and a(2:3) is a section of it. This is a big part of why Fortran is pleasant for maths.
sections.code:
program whole
  implicit none
  integer :: a(4), b(4)
  a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
  b = a * 10 + 1
  print '(*(i0, 1x))', b
  print '(i0)', sum(a)
  print '(i0)', maxval(b)
  print '(i0)', size(a)
  print '(*(i0, 1x))', a(2:3)
end program whole

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  integer :: a(3)
  a = [7, 8, 9]
  print '(i0)', a(1)
end program q1
practice.why: Fortran arrays start at index 1 by default, so a(1) is the first element.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  integer :: a(3)
  a = [1, 2, 3]
  a = a * a
  print '(*(i0, 1x))', a
end program q2
practice.why: a * a multiplies element by element: 1×1, 2×2, 3×3.

practice.code:
program q3
  implicit none
  integer :: a(5)
  a = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
  print '(i0)', sum(a(2:4))
end program q3
practice.why: a(2:4) is the section 4, 3, 2, which adds up to 9.

practice.q: How do you double every element of a real array x?
practice.why: Arithmetic on a whole array applies to every element, so no loop is needed.

sections.p: Procedures go after contains, at the end of the program. A function returns a value; a subroutine does not and is run with call. intent(in) promises an argument is only read, and intent(inout) lets the subroutine change the caller's variable.
sections.code:
program procs
  implicit none
  integer :: stash
  stash = 10
  print '(i0)', square(6)
  call add_nuts(stash, 5)
  print '(i0)', stash
contains
  function square(n) result(r)
    integer, intent(in) :: n
    integer :: r
    r = n * n
  end function square

  subroutine add_nuts(total, extra)
    integer, intent(inout) :: total
    integer, intent(in) :: extra
    total = total + extra
  end subroutine add_nuts
end program procs

sections.p: An argument declared x(:) takes an array of any length, and size(x) tells you how long it is. This is how library routines are written.
sections.code:
program mean_demo
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  print '(f0.2)', mean([2.0_real64, 4.0_real64, 9.0_real64])
contains
  function mean(x) result(m)
    real(real64), intent(in) :: x(:)
    real(real64) :: m
    m = sum(x) / size(x)
  end function mean
end program mean_demo

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  print '(i0)', twice(4) + 1
contains
  function twice(n) result(r)
    integer, intent(in) :: n
    integer :: r
    r = 2 * n
  end function twice
end program q1
practice.why: twice(4) is 8, and 1 is added after the call.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  n = 3
  call bump(n)
  call bump(n)
  print '(i0)', n
contains
  subroutine bump(k)
    integer, intent(inout) :: k
    k = k + 10
  end subroutine bump
end program q2
practice.why: Arguments are passed by reference, so each call adds 10 to the caller's n.

practice.q: How do you run a subroutine?
practice.why: Subroutines are run with call. Functions are used inside expressions.

practice.q: What does intent(in) mean on an argument?
options: The procedure only reads it and may not change it
It is an input from the keyboard
practice.answer: The procedure only reads it and may not change it
practice.why: The compiler checks the promise and reports an error if the procedure assigns to it.

lessons.title: Modules and derived types
lessons.summary: type, module, use and components with %.

sections.p: A derived type groups related values, like a record. You declare it with type :: name ... end type, create variables of that type, and reach a field with %. A structure constructor name(field, field) fills one in a single expression.
sections.code:
program types_demo
  implicit none
  type :: point
    real :: x, y
  end type point
  type(point) :: a, b, mid
  a = point(2.0, 4.0)
  b = point(6.0, 8.0)
  mid%x = (a%x + b%x) / 2
  mid%y = (a%y + b%y) / 2
  print '(a, f0.1, a, f0.1)', 'mid ', mid%x, ', ', mid%y
  print '(f0.1)', a%x * b%y - a%y * b%x
end program types_demo

sections.p: A module holds types and procedures that several programs can share. Put the module in the same file (or a separate one), then use module_name at the top of the program. Procedures that belong with the type go after contains inside the module.
sections.code:
module stash_mod
  implicit none
  type :: stash
    character(len=12) :: owner
    integer :: count
  end type stash
contains
  function total(items) result(s)
    type(stash), intent(in) :: items(:)
    integer :: s, i
    s = 0
    do i = 1, size(items)
      s = s + items(i)%count
    end do
  end function total
end module stash_mod

program demo
  use stash_mod
  implicit none
  type(stash) :: bank(2)
  bank(1) = stash('Hazel', 12)
  bank(2) = stash('Pip', 7)
  print '(a, 1x, i0)', trim(bank(1)%owner), bank(1)%count
  print '(a, 1x, i0)', trim(bank(2)%owner), bank(2)%count
  print '(a, i0)', 'total ', total(bank)
end program demo

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  type :: pair
    integer :: a, b
  end type pair
  type(pair) :: p
  p = pair(3, 4)
  print '(i0)', p%a * p%b
end program q1
practice.why: p%a is 3 and p%b is 4, so the product is 12.

practice.code:
module m
  implicit none
contains
  function double(n) result(r)
    integer, intent(in) :: n
    integer :: r
    r = 2 * n
  end function double
end module m

program q2
  use m
  implicit none
  print '(i0)', double(7)
end program q2
practice.why: use m brings double into the program, and double(7) is 14.

practice.q: How do you read a component of a derived type variable t?
practice.why: Fortran uses % for components. The dot is for other languages.

options: Makes the module's public names available in this program
practice.answer: Makes the module's public names available in this program
practice.why: use is how Fortran imports a module. only: can limit which names come in.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.summary: open, write, read, iostat and close.

sections.p: open(newunit=u, file=..., status=..., action=...) connects a unit number to a file. newunit asks the runtime for a free unit. write(u, format) ... and read(u, ...) use that unit. Always close(u) when finished. List-directed read(u, *) is handy for simple text files of words and numbers.
sections.code:
program fileio
  implicit none
  integer :: u, n, ios, total
  character(len=12) :: name
  open(newunit=u, file='nuts.txt', status='replace', action='write')
  write(u, '(a, 1x, i0)') 'acorn', 12
  write(u, '(a, 1x, i0)') 'walnut', 5
  write(u, '(a, 1x, i0)') 'hazel', 9
  close(u)
  open(newunit=u, file='nuts.txt', status='old', action='read')
  total = 0
  do
    read(u, *, iostat=ios) name, n
    if (ios /= 0) exit
    print '(a, a, i0)', trim(name), ' => ', n
    total = total + n
  end do
  close(u)
  print '(a, i0)', 'total ', total
end program fileio

sections.p: position='append' on an existing file adds at the end. On read, iostat becomes non-zero at end of file (or on an error); testing it is the usual way to stop a read loop without crashing.
sections.code:
program append_io
  implicit none
  integer :: u
  character(len=20) :: line
  integer :: ios
  open(newunit=u, file='log.txt', status='replace', action='write')
  write(u, '(a)') 'day 1: found 3'
  close(u)
  open(newunit=u, file='log.txt', status='old', position='append', action='write')
  write(u, '(a)') 'day 2: found 5'
  close(u)
  open(newunit=u, file='log.txt', status='old', action='read')
  do
    read(u, '(a)', iostat=ios) line
    if (ios /= 0) exit
    print '(a)', trim(line)
  end do
  close(u)
end program append_io

practice.code:
program q1
  implicit none
  integer :: u, n, ios, total
  open(newunit=u, file='t.txt', status='replace', action='write')
  write(u, '(i0)') 4
  write(u, '(i0)') 5
  close(u)
  open(newunit=u, file='t.txt', status='old', action='read')
  total = 0
  do
    read(u, *, iostat=ios) n
    if (ios /= 0) exit
    total = total + n
  end do
  close(u)
  print '(i0)', total
end program q1
practice.why: The file holds 4 and 5 on separate lines; the loop adds them.

practice.code:
program q2
  implicit none
  integer :: u, ios
  character(len=8) :: line
  open(newunit=u, file='a.txt', status='replace', action='write')
  write(u, '(a)') 'oak'
  close(u)
  open(newunit=u, file='a.txt', status='old', position='append', action='write')
  write(u, '(a)') 'elm'
  close(u)
  open(newunit=u, file='a.txt', status='old', action='read')
  do
    read(u, '(a)', iostat=ios) line
    if (ios /= 0) exit
    print '(a)', trim(line)
  end do
  close(u)
end program q2
practice.why: append adds elm after the existing oak line.

practice.q: What does iostat /= 0 usually mean on a read loop?
options: End of file (or an error) — time to exit
practice.answer: End of file (or an error) — time to exit
practice.why: A successful read sets iostat to 0. Non-zero ends the loop.

practice.q: What does status='replace' do on open?
options: Creates the file, or overwrites it if it exists
Opens only if the file already exists
practice.answer: Creates the file, or overwrites it if it exists
practice.why: replace is the usual choice when writing a fresh output file.

lessons.title: Project: a numerical nut tally
lessons.summary: Arrays, totals by tree, percentages and a mean.

sections.p: Five finds, each a tree name and a mass in kilograms, are totalled by tree. A small parallel array of kinds grows as new tree names appear; each find adds to that kind's running total. The report shows kilograms and a whole-number percentage of the grand total, then the mean find and the grand total — a miniature of the summary tables scientific codes print after a run.
sections.code:
program nut_tally
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 5
  character(len=8) :: tree(n)
  real(real64) :: kg(n), totals(3), grand
  character(len=8) :: kinds(3)
  integer :: i, k, nkinds
  tree = [character(len=8) :: 'oak', 'elm', 'oak', 'pine', 'elm']
  kg = [1.5_real64, 0.8_real64, 2.1_real64, 1.2_real64, 0.4_real64]
  nkinds = 0
  totals = 0.0_real64
  do i = 1, n
    do k = 1, nkinds
      if (kinds(k) == tree(i)) exit
    end do
    if (k > nkinds) then
      nkinds = nkinds + 1
      kinds(nkinds) = tree(i)
      k = nkinds
    end if
    totals(k) = totals(k) + kg(i)
  end do
  grand = sum(totals(1:nkinds))
  do k = 1, nkinds
    print '(a, 1x, f0.1, a, i0, a)', trim(kinds(k)), totals(k), &
      ' kg ', nint(100.0_real64 * totals(k) / grand), '%'
  end do
  print '(a, f0.2)', 'mean ', grand / real(n, real64)
  print '(a, f0.1)', 'total ', grand
end program nut_tally
sections.out:
oak 3.6 kg 60%
elm 1.2 kg 20%
pine 1.2 kg 20%
mean 1.20
total 6.0

sections.p: Wrap the find in a derived type inside a module, read the finds from a text file with read and iostat, or print the largest single find with maxloc.

practice.why: The loop adds every find into the matching kind's total.

practice.q: What does nint do for the percentages?
options: Rounds to the nearest whole number
practice.answer: Rounds to the nearest whole number
practice.why: nint(60.0) is 60, which prints cleanly with i0.

practice.code:
program q1
  use iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  implicit none
  real(real64) :: x(3)
  x = [1.0_real64, 2.0_real64, 3.0_real64]
  print '(f0.1)', sum(x) / size(x)
end program q1
practice.why: The mean of 1, 2 and 3 is 2.0.
